  • CBS News Baltimore · Nearly 25,000 federal workers in Maryland lost their jobs in 2025, data shows — A local read on the same national reduction in a federal-worker-heavy state.
  • Axios · Charted: The sharp decline in federal employment — Charts the 2025 fall in federal employment as the deferred-resignation departures landed.
  • Staffing Industry Analysts · October US Jobs Report: Pre-Shutdown Data and Alternative Indicators — Notes the October 2025 government shutdown disrupted federal data collection around the same release.

item.title: One UN road-safety target fell due in 2020, not 2030 — halve road deaths. We read WHO's rate estimates for the 183 economies it models: 13 halved their road-death rate, 71 got worse, and the global rate fell 8%
item.description: SDG target 3.6 set a rare 2020 deadline. Measured 2010 to 2019, the deepest cuts were concentrated in Gulf and Central Asian economies that started with high death rates — while Western Europe, generally starting far lower, largely did not halve, and the United States moved the wrong way, 11.7 to 12.7 per 100,000.
item.content:encoded:
The Facts

In 2015 every UN member state adopted Sustainable Development Goal 3.6: 'By 2020, halve the number of global deaths and injuries from road traffic accidents.' It is one of the few SDG targets that came due in 2020, not 2030. The target was not met; in 2020 the UN General Assembly proclaimed a new 2021-2030 Decade of Action, with a goal of reducing road-traffic deaths and injuries by at least 50% (resolution A/RES/74/299) — the horizon the World Health Organization now cites.

We pulled WHO's modeled road-traffic mortality rate — deaths per 100,000 people — from the World Bank series SH.STA.TRAF.P5 (source: WHO; last updated 2026-07-13; latest modeled year 2019) for every economy carrying a value at both the 2010 baseline and 2019, the last full year WHO modeled before the deadline. 183 of the world's 217 economies qualify.

Across those 183, the global rate fell from 18.2 to 16.7 deaths per 100,000 — an 8.0% drop, about one-sixth of the way to halving. Thirteen economies actually halved their rate. Another 98 fell by less than half, 71 rose, and one held level; the median economy cut its rate 7.7%.

The deep cuts came from economies that began the decade with very high death rates. Oman went from 27.8 to 10.6, Kazakhstan 25.9 to 12.7, Belarus 21.9 to 7.6, the United Arab Emirates 19.4 to 8.9 — joined by Qatar, Bahrain, Trinidad and Tobago and Montenegro, all economies whose 2010 rates ranked among the highest on record. Eight of the thirteen halvers were high-income; only one was lower-middle income, and none were low-income.

The Analysis

The following is analysis, not fact. The pledge reads as a universal ambition; the record reads as a story about starting points. The economies that halved were mostly the ones with the most distance to fall — high-rate Gulf and post-Soviet states cutting from double-digit tolls. Western Europe and Japan, generally starting from much lower rates, largely did not halve: the United Kingdom moved 3.7 to 3.2, Germany 4.8 to 3.8, Japan 5.3 to 3.6, France 6.5 to 5.1, while Sweden and the Netherlands barely moved. Not one of them halved.

The vantage a single national desk structurally cannot see is direction across the whole set: 71 economies — more than a third of the 183 — ended the decade worse than they began it. The United States is a prominent rich-country exception in the wrong direction, its rate rising from 11.7 to 12.7 — already several times its major European peers' and still climbing. The largest wrong-way move on the board is the Dominican Republic, from 27.8 to 64.6, and Saudi Arabia, a high-income state, rose 45%. Why any one country moved as it did is not something these figures isolate — the ranking is the finding, not a mechanism these data test. sspeculative

Room for Disagreement

Two cautions. First, metric: the SDG target counts deaths; we measured the per-100,000 rate, the standard cross-country comparator. The two diverge because population and traffic grew underneath the rate. WHO's own count-based tally has annual road deaths falling 5%, to 1.19 million in 2021, and names 10 countries — not our 13 — that cut the number of deaths by at least half; its endpoint is 2021 and ours 2019, its metric the count and ours the rate. By either yardstick the 2020 target was missed. Second, these are modeled estimates with wide uncertainty bands: the tiny-island swings (Tonga up more than fourfold, Micronesia to near zero) sit inside the noise, and the clearest large moves in the point estimates include the Gulf and Central Asian halvers, the US and Dominican Republic risers, though those estimates carry uncertainty too. sspeculative

The View From

**View from WHO:** the tally is heading downward but nowhere near fast enough, in the words of its director-general; the agency frames road crashes as the leading killer of people aged 5–29 and notes 92% of deaths fall in low- and middle-income countries — and it has folded the missed 2020 goal into a 2030 one. mmodeled **View from a high-income capital:** a rate already among the world's lowest leaves little left to halve, and a plateau near 3–5 per 100,000 can reflect a road system near its practical floor rather than complacency. sspeculative The reading that resists this defense is the United States, whose rate rose from an already-high base while its peers held or fell.

Notable

  • International Road Federation · Despite notable progress, road safety remains an urgent global issue — Industry-body coverage of the WHO 2023 report that anchors this piece — the missed target framed from the road-safety sector.
  • Global Alliance of NGOs for Road Safety · Global Status Report on Road Safety 2023 launched — Subject-matter coverage of the report launch and its 2010-to-2021 findings.
  • Vital Strategies · New data proves we can reduce global road deaths, but the alarming loss of life demands urgent uptake of proven interventions — Public-health-group statement reading the same WHO figures the country-by-country counts here are drawn from.
  • Asia Pacific Road Safety Observatory · Launch of the WHO Global Status Report on Road Safety 2023 — Regional road-safety observatory coverage of the report and the decade-long trend.

item.title: The Federal Register shed 39% of its pages in 2025 but only 14% of its documents — its output fell far more in length than in count — and 2026 has won back about half the pages
item.description: Read by the same Aug. 25 cutoff every year, the Register printed 68,242 pages in 2024, 41,501 in 2025 — its second-lowest count in a decade, behind only 2017 — and 54,935 in 2026. The document count barely tracked the swing: 18,766, then 16,140, then 16,949. Average pages per document fell from 3.64 to 2.57 and back to 3.24, while notices held a flat ~81% share throughout.
item.content:encoded:
The Facts

The Federal Register numbers its pages consecutively from the first business day of each calendar year, so the last page printed on any given date is a running odometer of how much the government has published so far that year. We read that odometer at the same cutoff — the last issue on or before Aug. 25 — for each of the last ten years, straight from the Federal Register's own API, and paired it with the exact document counts the API returns for the same Jan. 1–Aug. 25 window.

By that cutoff the page count ran 40,666 (2017), 42,984 (2018), 44,535 (2019), 52,420 (2020), 47,540 (2021), 52,430 (2022), 58,440 (2023), 68,242 (2024), 41,501 (2025) and 54,935 (2026). Two readings stand out. 2024 is the decade high. 2025's 41,501 is the second-lowest of the ten — only 2017 printed fewer by this date — a 39% drop from the year before.

The document count did not fall nearly as far. Counting every document the Register published in each window — rules, proposed rules, notices and presidential documents — the totals were 18,209 (2023), 18,766 (2024), 16,140 (2025) and 16,949 (2026). From 2024 to 2025 the page count fell 39.2% while the document count fell 14.0%; the pages behind each document dropped from 3.64 to 2.57, a 29% thinning. The mix did not move: notices were 81.9% of all documents in 2024, 80.7% in 2025 and 80.4% in 2026, so the shorter average is not a swing toward short filings.

Underneath, the pieces moved unevenly. Final rules fell from 2,037 in the 2024 window to 1,668 in 2025 (−18.1%), then recovered to 1,947 in 2026. Presidential documents ran the other way — 177 in the 2024 window, then 376 in 2025 (a new-term surge of executive orders and proclamations), back to 176 in 2026 — which propped up the 2025 document total even as rules and notices thinned. In 2026 the page odometer, 54,935, sits about halfway between 2025's floor and 2024's peak, and pages-per-document, at 3.24, has recovered about two-thirds of the length lost the year before.

The Analysis

The following is analysis, not fact. Page count and document count are different instruments, and 2025 is the year they came apart. A notice of a hearing runs a page or two; a major final rule carries a preamble, a response to public comments and a cost-benefit analysis that can run into the hundreds of pages. So the total page count is dominated by the handful of long, consequential rules, while the document count is dominated by the ~81% of filings that are short notices. When pages fall almost three times as fast as documents, the drop is concentrated in the page-dense material — the long rules and their preambles — rather than spread evenly across the short notices that dominate the count. Whether that means fewer big rules or shorter ones, the page odometer and document count alone cannot separate; both would produce this same signature sspeculative.

Outside trackers that count the narrower slice directly report the same shape: the Competitive Enterprise Institute recorded 68 economically significant rules (those with $100 million-plus in effects) by mid-2025, against 342 in 2023, and the George Washington Regulatory Studies Center's series shows 2024 finishing at a record 106,109 full-year pages before the 2025 reversal [modeled — their tallies, on definitions and windows that differ from ours]. The drop also coincides with a documented administrative act: the Jan. 20, 2025 'Regulatory Freeze Pending Review' memorandum, the kind of government-wide pause every incoming administration since 2001 has issued, designed to delay effective dates and capable of holding down early-year output. That the memo exists and took effect is documented; that it drove this particular 39% drop is an inference we cannot isolate from ordinary first-year deregulatory posture or other factors sspeculative. And 2026's rebound is mostly length returning, not a document surge: the document count rose 5.0% while pages rose 32.4%, so the average filing got longer again rather than the government filing far more of them.

Room for Disagreement

Page count is a blunt proxy and it is most of what we measured. A single 500-page rule can swing the odometer more than a thousand routine notices, so a low page count can mean 'no large rules this year' rather than 'less governing' — and it says nothing about the economic weight or burden of what did publish. The George Washington Regulatory Studies Center's longer-run finding cuts the other way from any 'shrinking rulebook' read: across 1995–2020 the number of rules fell while their average length rose, agencies bundling more into fewer, larger rulemakings. Our 2025 snapshot is a deregulatory-year reversal of that trend, not evidence against it.

Two more limits. Both endpoints are read at a partial-year Aug. 25 cutoff; full-year 2026 could land anywhere, and cutoff-to-cutoff comparisons carry the noise of blank pages, corrections and issue timing. And pages-per-document across all four document types is a composite — the clean statement is the divergence itself (pages −39% vs documents −14% into 2025), not the ratio, since the ratio can move on the notice/rule mix alone. Every figure here is scoped to the Jan. 1–Aug. 25 window of its year.

Notable

  • GW Regulatory Studies Center · Federal Agencies are Publishing Fewer but Larger Regulations — The structural counterpoint, 1995–2020: rule counts fell while average rule length rose, agencies consolidating into fewer, larger rulemakings. Our 2025 finding (pages fell far faster than documents) is a deregulatory-year reversal of that long trend, and this is the steelman in our disagreement block.
  • Competitive Enterprise Institute · The year the red tape died? Trump's 2025 rule count hits historic lows — External reporting on the 2025 collapse: 28,799 Register pages and 1,255 rules by July 1, 2025, against a record 106,109 pages and 3,248 rules in Biden's final year; economically significant rules down to 68 from 342 in 2023 — the narrower slice that corroborates our 'big rules thinned fastest' read.
  • American Action Forum · 2025: The Year in Regulation — Independent year-in-review tracking of 2025 rulemaking volume and cost, a second external tally against which our page-and-document counts can be checked.
  • GW Regulatory Studies Center · Reg Stats — Total Pages Published in the Federal Register — The established full-year page-count series back to 1936, which records 2024 as the modern high; context for why our same-cutoff 2024 reading is the decade peak and 2025's is a sharp reversal.

item.title: We read all 33 NFL preseason games so far: scoring peaks in the second quarter and craters in the third
item.description: The fourth quarter, played almost entirely by backups, outscored the starters' opening quarter by 78 points. The scoring doesn't follow the talent off the field.
item.content:encoded:
The Facts

We added up every quarter of every NFL preseason game played so far this August — all 33 of them, from the Aug. 7 Hall of Fame Game through the round that ended Aug. 24, the two exhibition weekends that come before the final dress-rehearsal round. Together they scored 1,200 points.

Sorted by quarter, the scoring is lopsided: 244 in the first, 434 in the second, 200 in the third, 322 in the fourth. The second quarter alone holds 36% of all the points and outscores the third by better than two to one — 2.17x. The first half outscored the second, 678 to 522, but the shape inside is not a slide. It is a peak, a crater, and a rebound.

The fourth quarter — played almost entirely by backups and roster-bubble players — outscored the first quarter, the starters' quarter, by 78 points, 322 to 244. And the pattern is not one loud weekend: read the two exhibition rounds separately, and in each the second quarter is the highest- scoring and the third the lowest. Of the 33 games, 16 were within one score entering the fourth quarter and 13 finished within one.

Every quarter figure re-derives from a frozen capture of the ESPN scoreboard (seasontype 1, weeks 1–3, retrieved Aug. 25, 2026; five re-pulls returned identical final box scores), SHA-256 c485776e…d609d47.

The Analysis

The following is analysis, not fact. The broadcast intuition about a preseason game is a slide: the starters open, the talent bleeds off the field drive by drive, and by the fourth quarter you are watching players who will be cut on Tuesday. Scoring, the intuition says, should fall as the roster empties.

The whole-record read says it doesn't. Scoring climbs to its high right before halftime, collapses to less than half of that in the third quarter, then climbs back up in the fourth — the quarter with the least NFL talent on the field outscoring the quarter with the most. The number that carries the story is the third quarter: 200 points, the fewest of any frame, in the stretch right after the break when you would expect fresh legs, not the fewest points of the night.

A plausible read of the shape — offered as hypothesis, not proof — is that the second-quarter spike is a two-minute-drill artifact, offenses pushing to score before the half while the best available players are still in, and that the fourth-quarter rebound is roster-bubble urgency: players auditioning for jobs, in a hurry, against a defense doing the same sspeculative. The third quarter is the dead zone in between — wholesale substitutions, feeling-out, no one yet desperate sspeculative. What the data pins down is the timing, not the cause: the points arrive on a curve the box score never plots, and it is not the curve the talent chart would draw.

Room for Disagreement

This is 33 games, and preseason is a small, noisy sample — a few garbage-time drives can move a single quarter's total. More important, the read stops one round short of the whole: the dress-rehearsal round, when starters traditionally stay in through the third quarter, is scheduled for Aug. 27–29 and is not in this count. If starters do play deeper in that round, the third-quarter crater could flatten — the pattern here belongs to the two early rounds, when most first units were done by halftime, and should not be sold as a law of the whole preseason. The second-quarter peak may also owe as much to clock mechanics as to who is on the field.

Notable

  • CBS Sports · 2026 NFL Game Scores — Preseason — Independent scoreboard of the same games.
  • Bleacher Report · Breaking Down the Progression of the NFL Preseason — Context: the customary snap progression — starters into Q1 early, into Q3 by the dress rehearsal, rested in the finale.
  • StatButler · A Brief Guide to Preseason Playing Time — Context: how little of a preseason game the starters actually play.

item.title: We priced all 31,210 fantasy opportunities of 2025: in PPR a target is worth 2.64 carries, 1.60 in standard
item.description: A carry and a target are the two atoms of fantasy scoring, and they are not priced alike. Read the complete 2025 ledger and the gap holds even inside the running-back pool — the 55 backs with 100-plus opportunities ran on 81% of their chances but banked only 63% of their points there, and made the other 37% on the 19% that came through the air.
item.content:encoded:
The Facts

A single-team manager counts touches as one number: my back got 20, my receiver got 8. Read the complete 2025 opportunity ledger and that number is two different currencies quietly added together. In nflverse's full 2025 regular-season file — every player, all 18 weeks — the NFL logged 14,601 rushing carries and 16,609 pass targets, 31,210 opportunities in all, and they do not pay the same.

Priced in full-PPR scoring (0.1 per rushing or receiving yard, 6 per touchdown, 1.0 per catch), the average carry returned 0.645 fantasy points and the average target 1.705 — a target was worth 2.64 carries. The gap is set by the rulebook, not the field: strip the reception point and run the same 2025 season in standard scoring and a target falls to 1.60 carries; half-PPR puts it at 2.12. Restrict the count to the running backs, receivers and tight ends managers actually draft and the full-PPR ratio rises to 2.7.

The tell is that the gap survives inside a single position, where preference can't explain it. The 55 running backs who cleared 100 opportunities in 2025 took 81.3% of their chances as carries — but those carries produced only 63.4% of their fantasy points, while the 18.7% that came as targets produced 36.6%. Christian McCaffrey finished the overall PPR RB1 on 311 carries and 129 targets; Jonathan Taylor carried a league-high 323 times at 0.958 points per opportunity, and James Cook — 309 carries against 40 targets — ran on 88.5% of his chances, among the most carry-dependent workloads in the pool, at 0.883 points per opportunity.

The Analysis

The following is analysis, not fact. The opportunity-versus-output spine of fantasy football usually gets read as a question of how much: how many carries, how many targets. The 2025 ledger says the prior question is what kind. A carry and a target are both usage — both volume a manager accumulates across a season mmodeled — and both show up in the same touch column — but one books a point the instant the ball is caught, before a yard is gained, and the other does not. At the league's 67.5% catch rate — a reception on roughly two of every three targets — that reception point alone lifts the average target most of the way to its 2.64-carry price.

That is why the running-back split matters more than the cross-position one. It would be easy to read 1.705 versus 0.645 as receivers simply out-earning runners. But the same kind of gap — wider still — opens inside one back's own stat line: 29% of McCaffrey's opportunities came through the air, and they produced 57% of his fantasy points, a target worth 3.16 carries to him. The manager adding a carry and a catch into one touch total is adding two numbers denominated in different units, and weighting them equally understates the target pile.

Room for Disagreement

Per opportunity is not per season. Running backs still crowd the top of PPR boards precisely because they command the volume: McCaffrey saw 440 opportunities in 2025 to the most-used receiver's 188 (ranking receivers by total opportunities), and a rate disadvantage loses to that much raw usage. The ratio is also a scoring-rules artifact, not a law of football — it collapses toward 1.60 in standard leagues, so half of the point here is about how a commissioner set the scoring, and league settings vary. And a carry can carry value this per-opportunity frame doesn't capture: short-yardage and goal-line carries are widely modeled as worth more than the average one, carries drain the game clock, and rushing volume is conventionally steadier week to week than target volume, which depends on staying on the field for pass downs. Those are established characterizations of the position, not measurements in this season-total ledger, which captures neither leverage nor week-to-week variance mmodeled. This is the completed 2025 record, not a projection of 2026.

The View From

From inside one roster, a touch is a touch and 20 beats 8. From the whole 2025 ledger, the two atoms of that count are priced 2.64 to 1 in PPR — and the season's most carry-heavy backs banked their smallest slice of work at the highest rate.

Notable

  • PFF · Metrics that Matter: The value of a carry, the value of a target — The canonical trade-press treatment of the same question; it puts the decade-long PPR figure at a target worth 2.74 carries — the established rule of thumb this 2025-only measurement sits inside.
  • Fantasy Points · Statistically Significant: Weighted Opportunity — Analyst work on weighting a target above a carry when scoring opportunity (paywalled) — the modeling tradition behind expected-points and weighted-opportunity metrics.
  • Pro Football Network · What Is the PPR Scoring System in Fantasy Football? — Background explainer on the reception point — the single scoring rule that drives the carry-versus-target gap measured here.
  • FantasyPros · Beginner's Guide to Understanding Fantasy Football League Scoring Systems — Contemporaneous 2026 rundown of standard, half-PPR and full-PPR formats — the three settings that price a target at 1.60, 2.12 and 2.64 carries in this data.
  • ESPN · PPR fantasy football: Which players see value increases and decreases — Market-side coverage of how the reception point re-sorts player value between scoring formats.

item.title: Read by function, not by agency, the second-largest increase in federal spending through July was interest
item.description: We pulled the Monthly Treasury Statement's functional ledger, which files spending by purpose rather than by department. Of 19 budget functions, net interest added $90.6 billion year-over-year — the largest increase of any function except Medicare, and more than Social Security, defense or veterans' care. The department ledger hides it inside Treasury; this one puts it on its own line.
item.content:encoded:
The Facts

Federal spending is published two ways, and they classify the same dollars differently. One ledger sorts outlays by the department that spends them — interest lands inside Treasury, Medicare inside Health and Human Services. The other sorts them by function: what the money is for. We pulled the second one, Table 9 of the Treasury's Monthly Treasury Statement, for record_date 2026-07-31 (fiscal 2026 through July), with each function's prior-year figure printed beside it.

Total net outlays through July were $6,284.2 billion, up $309.1 billion — 5.2% — from $5,975.2 billion in the same 10 months of fiscal 2025.

Sorted by function, one line grew more than any other except Medicare: net interest rose $90.6 billion, to $931.4 billion from $840.8 billion, a 10.8% increase. That single function accounts for 29.3% of the government's entire $309.1 billion spending increase. Only Medicare grew more — up $131.1 billion (+15.9%). Together, Medicare and net interest added $221.7 billion, 71.7% of the net rise.

Net interest grew more than the functions usually named as the drivers of federal spending. Social Security rose $70.7 billion, national defense $45.7 billion, the separate Health function $39.8 billion, and veterans' benefits $50.6 billion — each less than interest's $90.6 billion. The counter-current was Education, Training, Employment and Social Services, down $81.6 billion (to $82.0 billion from $163.7 billion), the largest decline of any function — a swing addressed in the caution below.

By level, not just growth, net interest is now the third-largest function of government: Social Security $1,384.4 billion, Medicare $954.5 billion, net interest $931.4 billion, Health $845.2 billion, national defense $803.7 billion. Interest sits $23.1 billion below Medicare and $127.7 billion above defense.

One precision the functional ledger forces: its net interest ($931.4 billion) is not the same figure as the department ledger's gross interest on the public debt, which runs higher. The function is net — gross interest less the interest the government collects, chiefly intragovernmental interest credited to trust funds. The two ledgers describe the same obligation at different points; this piece uses the net function throughout.

The Analysis

The following is analysis, not fact. The number itself — net interest up $90.6 billion — is arithmetic off two published columns. What the functional cut adds is where that number sits, and the answer is that it sits in a place the department ledger cannot show it. Read by department, interest is a subline inside a $1.4-trillion Treasury total, and Medicare is folded into Health and Human Services; neither stands alone. Read by function, both step out, and the two of them together carry nearly three-quarters of a year's spending growth.

What separates net interest from the other four large risers is not its size — Medicare grew more — but that no one sets its level. Interest is paid under a permanent, indefinite appropriation that needs no annual vote; the big entitlements, Social Security and Medicare, are mandatory too, but their spending flows from benefit formulas Congress writes and can change, and defense is appropriated year by year. Net interest answers to neither a benefit formula nor an annual vote — it is the arithmetic product of the debt outstanding and the rates it carries, rising with the debt stock and the market whether or not anyone acts mmodeled. We do not, from this table, attribute the $90.6 billion to any single cause; a rise in net interest can come from a larger debt stock, higher rates on the parts that reprice, or a change in the interest the government receives, and Table 9 separates none of these. The delta is the fact; the mechanism is not one this ledger isolates.

Read the two ledgers side by side and the same 10 months tell two stories. The department view, which a release-day desk is likelier to run, shows spending concentrated in a few big agencies. The functional view shows one of those concentrations is simply the cost of carrying the debt — a line that is now the third-largest thing the government does and, by dollars, its second-largest increase.

Room for Disagreement

The sharpest caution is that this is the same $309.1 billion increase visible in the department ledger, re-sorted — not a second, independent finding. Whether net interest ranks second or third among growth drivers depends partly on the taxonomy: the functional ledger splits Medicare from the broader Health function. By level it is steadier — combining the two health functions ($1,799.7 billion) would leave net interest third, changing only what sits above it, not its rank. The robust claim is the delta itself — net interest up $90.6 billion, larger than any function's increase but Medicare's — not a ranking that shifts with how the categories are drawn.

Second, the Education function's $81.6 billion decline should not be read as an $82 billion cut to schools. Net outlays for credit-heavy functions fold in credit-subsidy re-estimates under the Federal Credit Reform Act, which can swing a student-loan line by tens of billions in a year without a matching change in activity; the drop reads best as net accounting, not a halving of services mmodeled.

Third, these are 10-month, year-to-date figures, not full-year results, and nominal dollars — a 5.2% nominal rise is smaller after inflation. Fiscal 2026 still has August and September to run, and the September close can reshuffle function totals.

The View From

From the topline, fiscal 2026 reads as ordinary growth: outlays up 5.2%, a wider deficit, the usual entitlement pressure. Sorted by what the money is for, the same 10 months put the cost of the debt itself among the government's three largest activities and its second-largest increase by dollars — a line that grew more than defense, more than Social Security, and second only to Medicare — one that answers to the debt outstanding and the rate market rather than to any benefit formula or budget vote. The figure that reads as routine and the function quietly climbing the table are the same statement, sorted two ways.

Notable

  • U.S. Department of the Treasury · Monthly Treasury Statement — Receipts and Outlays of the U.S. Government — The Bureau of the Fiscal Service's monthly release; the primary document whose Table 9 (summary of receipts and outlays by function) is the basis for every figure here. Re-pull the July 2026 statement to reproduce the 19 functional lines and the $6,284.2 billion total.
  • U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data · Monthly Treasury Statement — Summary of Receipts and Outlays by Function (dataset) — The machine-readable dataset behind this piece; query record_date 2026-07-31 in mts_table_9 to see each function's current and prior year-to-date figure without the API.
  • U.S. Treasury Fiscal Data · Fiscal Data API documentation — Documents the endpoint and filters used for every pull this run (mts_table_9, filtered by record_date), so any reader can reproduce the functional lines and the year-over-year deltas.
  • Congressional Budget Office · Monthly Budget Review — CBO's independent monthly reconstruction of federal receipts and outlays; the standard external cross-check on the Treasury totals and on the growth of net interest relative to program spending.
  • U.S. Government Accountability Office · America's Fiscal Future — Federal Spending — Background on the composition of federal outlays and why net interest, which no annual appropriation sets, is projected to grow faster than most program functions.
  • Office of Management and Budget · Budget of the U.S. Government — Historical Tables (functional classification) — Defines the functional classification the MTS follows — how outlays are sorted by purpose (national defense, health, Medicare, net interest) rather than by department — the taxonomy this piece relies on and whose Medicare-vs-Health split the caution flags.

item.title: The UK updated 206 of its 226 travel-advice pages on one December day with the same sentence — and for 38 countries it is still the newest change
item.description: Read one country page and the update date looks like fresh local intelligence. Read all 226 at once and it resolves into a single note about British dual nationals, pasted across the world in a day — the third time since 2020 one sentence has landed on 200-plus pages at once.
item.content:encoded:
The Facts

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office publishes travel advice for 226 countries and territories, each on its own page with a prominent last-updated date and a public change log. We pulled all 226 pages through the gov.uk content API on 25 August 2026 and read every page's `change_history` array — FCDO's own dated record of every edit.

On 10 December 2025, 206 of the 226 pages logged the same dual-nationals change: 'New information about dual nationals returning to the UK (Entry requirements page).' On 201 of them that sentence stands alone, give or take a stray space; the other 5 — Burundi, Cyprus, Iran, Tanzania and Ukraine — fold the identical dual-nationals line into a longer country-specific entry.

211 pages carry that note somewhere in their history. The 15 that never received it are 13 British Overseas Territories and Crown-linked pages — where 'returning to the UK' reads differently — plus India and Venezuela, which logged their own edits instead.

For 38 of the 226 pages, that 10 December paste is still the most recent entry in the log as of 25 August 2026 — more than eight months with no country-specific change. The 38 include North Korea, Haiti, Nicaragua, Moldova, Namibia, Burkina Faso and Uruguay.

It is not a one-off. On 8 June 2020, 211 pages logged an identical note on rules for entering the UK; on 22 June 2023, 225 logged an identical global-terrorism note. Three times in six years, one sentence has reached 200-plus pages in a single day. Across all 226 pages the median gap since the last edit is 63 days; 57 pages have gone more than 180.

The Analysis

The following is analysis, not fact. Every country page leads with a last-updated date, and on a single page that date reads as current, country-specific intelligence. Read across the whole set at once, and the date is frequently something else: a UK-side housekeeping edit applied everywhere the same morning — the same words on the Lesotho page, the Monaco page, the North Korea page and 203 others.

The 10 December note is a genuine change; it added real guidance about dual nationals. But it says nothing about conditions in the 206 destinations it landed on. A traveller checking Haiti or North Korea sees a December 2025 date and no cue that the substance was a global paste rather than a re-look at the country — an inference the record can flag but not measure. sspeculative

This is the inverse of a policy rollout. The EU's Entry/Exit System is a real border system reaching the borders it governs; a boilerplate note is the opposite motion — one administrative sentence reaching nearly the whole world regardless of any border. mmodeled

Room for Disagreement

FCDO updates by exception, and the exception process plainly works: pages for Norway, Jordan and South Sudan each changed the same morning we pulled them, and a 63-day median gap is not a stale system. For a settled destination, no news is the honest signal — and a bulk edit that genuinely adds dual-national guidance is a real change, not filler. FCDO never claims a fresh date means the whole assessment was rewritten; the last-updated stamp marks the last edit, which is exactly what these were. The gap here is between what the date says and what a hurried reader reads into it — not between the date and the truth.

The View From

From a traveller's desk: the update date is not a proxy for how current a country's risk picture is. Open the page's own Entry requirements and Safety and security sections, check when the substance — not the stamp — last moved, and confirm entry and visa rules against the destination's own authorities and your nearest embassy or consulate before you travel. A wrong assumption about entry rules can strand you at a border; the date on the page will not.

Notable

  • National Geographic · FCDO travel advice for U.K. travellers — explained — External explainer on how the FCDO advisory system works; independently states the same 226-country scope.
  • GOV.UK (context — FCDO methodology) · About Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office travel advice — FCDO's own account of how it updates advice — constantly reviewed, several updates a day during a crisis. Background, not third-party reporting.
  • GOV.UK (context — the advice set) · Foreign travel advice — The human-readable index of all 226 country and territory pages this piece read at scale.
  • European Commission (context — a real rollout, for contrast) · Entry/Exit System (EES) — A genuine border-policy change, unlike the worldwide boilerplate paste — the contrast the analysis draws.

item.title: The Federal Reserve sent the Treasury about $88 billion a year for the better part of a decade. Since September 2022 it has sent almost nothing — and its own balance sheet carries a $233 billion reason why.
item.description: Treasury's receipt line for Federal Reserve earnings collapsed from $106.7 billion in fiscal 2022 to $0.58 billion the next year. The Fed's own books explain it: a 'deferred asset' — the losses it must earn back before payments resume — that grew for more than three years to $245.9 billion, peaked in January 2026, and has only just begun to shrink.
item.content:encoded:
The Facts

For years the Federal Reserve was a quiet line in the Treasury's income. By law the Fed keeps only what it needs to operate and remits the rest of its earnings to the government; the Treasury books the money as a receipt. In the eight fiscal years 2015 through 2022 those remittances ran between $52.8 billion and $115.7 billion a year and averaged $88.2 billion — real money against the deficit, arriving weekly.

Then it stopped. We pulled the complete Monthly Treasury Statement series for the line 'Deposit of Earnings, Federal Reserve System.' It fell from $106.7 billion in fiscal 2022 to $0.58 billion in fiscal 2023 — a $106 billion receipt that all but vanished in a single year. It has stayed gone: $3.13 billion in fiscal 2024, $5.49 billion in fiscal 2025, and $8.47 billion through the first ten months of fiscal 2026 — up from $4.63 billion in the same ten months a year earlier, but still under a tenth of the old norm.

The reason sits on the Fed's own weekly balance sheet, the H.4.1. Its line 'Earnings remittances due to the U.S. Treasury' turned negative the week of September 7, 2022. A negative value there is the Fed's 'deferred asset' — an accounting marker for cumulative losses it must recover before it owes the Treasury anything again. It grew almost every week for more than three years: $18.0 billion by the end of 2022, $131.5 billion by the end of 2023, $215.2 billion by the end of 2024, and a peak of $245.9 billion on January 28, 2026. Across the remittance record we pulled — positive every year from 2015 through 2022 — the Fed had never carried a sustained deferred asset; this is the first.

Since that January peak it has shrunk — to $233.0 billion as of August 19, 2026, a decline of $13.0 billion over 203 days, or about $23 billion a year annualized.

The Analysis

The following is analysis, not fact. The Fed pays interest on the bank reserves and reverse-repurchase balances parked with it, and earns interest on the Treasury and mortgage bonds it bought during quantitative easing. When short-term rates climbed above the yields on that older portfolio, the first bill exceeded the second income, and the Fed began running an operating loss — the mechanism it points to for the deferred asset. Until the marker returns to zero, the weekly remittance to the Treasury is effectively switched off.

Two federal ledgers, read together, tell the whole story: the receipt the Treasury lost, and the $233 billion deferred-asset balance on the Fed's books that marks when it might come back. The small amounts still posting to Treasury's Fed-earnings line — $8.47 billion this year, nearly double last year's pace — do not, on their own, signal the full remittance returning sspeculative: a quarter-trillion-dollar deferred asset still stands ahead of any resumed transfer, and the two ledgers do not reconcile dollar-for-dollar.

The one genuinely new thing in the 2026 data is the turn: for the first time since 2022 the deferred asset is falling, not rising, as the Fed's net income swings back to positive. At the pace of its first seven months of decline it would take roughly a decade to clear — but that pace is a straight-line guess, not a forecast, and it hangs entirely on where interest rates go next sspeculative.

Room for Disagreement

The two ledgers do not reconcile dollar-for-dollar, and we are not forcing them to. Treasury's receipt line and the Fed's H.4.1 remittances-due line are different measures of the same relationship, kept on different bases; we report each as its source states it and flag, rather than paper over, the gap between the small deposits Treasury still books and the still-negative balance on the Fed's books.

The 'decade to clear' figure is the softest number here. It is a naive extrapolation of one seven-month stretch — we did not model the rate path, the pace of balance-sheet runoff, or the Fed's income, any of which could halve or double it sspeculative. And none of this is a loss to taxpayers in the ordinary sense: the deferred asset is an internal accounting device, not a debt the Fed must raise cash to repay. What it measures is a receipt the budget used to count on and no longer can — the opportunity cost, not a bill coming due mmodeled.

The View From

A single year's Treasury statement shows a Fed-earnings line near zero and little else. Reading the full receipt series back to 2015 against the Fed's entire weekly balance sheet is what turns that blank line into a number with a date on it: $233 billion, falling since January, roughly a decade from zero at the current crawl.

Notable

  • Federal Reserve Board · Federal Reserve Board announces Reserve Bank income and expense data and transfers to the Treasury for 2022 — Primary/methodology, not third-party reporting: the Fed's own release documenting the September 2022 suspension of remittances and how the deferred asset works.
  • Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis · The Fed's Remittances to the Treasury: Explaining the 'Deferred Asset' — Context/explainer: plain-language account of why remittances stopped when interest costs outran securities income.
  • FRED Blog (Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis) · Federal Reserve remittances to the US Treasury — Context: charts the historical remittance series and its drop to zero using the same FRED data underlying this piece.
  • Congressional Research Service · The Federal Reserve's Balance Sheet (In Focus IF12147) — Background: CRS primer on why the Fed operates at a loss — paying more on reserves and reverse repos than it earns on its QE-era holdings.
  • Bloomberg · Fed's Operating Losses Swelled to Record $114.3 Billion in 2023 — External reporting on the record operating loss that built the deferred asset (paywalled).
